In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds; the final outcome is for the God-fearing; prayers and peace be upon His Messenger Muhammad and all his family; and there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers. O Allah, bless and grant success.

Discourse on the Tafsir of the Opening Chapter (Fatihat al-Kitab)

The Shaykh, the Imam, the Greatest, the Ascetic, Jamal al-A'immah, Abu al-Muzaffar Mansur ibn Muhammad al-Sam'ani, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, said:

Know that this surah has four names: Fatihat al-Kitab (the Opening of the Book), Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an), al-Sab' al-Mathani (the Seven Oft-Repeated), and al-Sab' min al-Mathani (the Seven of the Oft-Repeated), related through the narration of 'Abd Khayr, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

As for Fatihat al-Kitab, it is because the Book, which is the Qur'an, is opened with it.

As for Umm al-Qur'an, it is because it is the origin of the Qur'an; from it the Qur'an began. The "umm" of a thing is its origin, and from this is said of Makkah, Umm al-Qura, because it is the origin of the cities.

As for al-Sab' al-Mathani, it is because it consists of seven verses by the agreement of the scholars, except in a single anomalous narration that says it has eight verses. It is called mathani because it is repeated (tuthna) in the prayer, so it is recited in every rak'ah.

Mujahid said: It is only called mathani because Allah the Exalted singled it out (istathnaha) for this Community, as if He revealed it to them and did not give it to any other nation.

As for al-Sab' min al-Mathani, there are two opinions concerning it. The first: that these are seven particular verses from the mathani, which is the Qur'an, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A Book that is consistent, repeating (mutashabihan mathani)﴾.

The Qur'an is called mathani because it contains sciences that are repeated, such as promise and threat, command and prohibition, and the like.

The second: that "al-sab' min al-mathani" is the same as "al-sab' al-mathani", and "min" in it is for emphasis (silah). This disagreement arose from the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated﴾.

Then know that this surah is Meccan according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas, while Mujahid said it is Medinan.

It is also said: it was revealed twice, once in Makkah and once in Madinah; and for this reason it is called mathani, because it was repeated in revelation. This is a strange narration.

His saying: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is a verse of the Fatihah according to the view of some scholars, and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Umm Salamah.

It is not a verse of it according to the view of others. This is mentioned with its evidence in jurisprudence (fiqh).

Then know that the letter ba' (ب) in His saying: ﴿bismi Allah﴾ is a particle that puts in the genitive what follows it from the speech, like min (from), 'an (about), fi (in), 'ala (upon), and their like.

The meaning attached to the ba' is indicated by the context, and its estimated sense is: "I begin with the name of Allah," or "I began with the name of Allah."

His saying: ﴿bismi Allah﴾ originally was bi-ism Allah, like His saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾. The alif was omitted in writing because it is not pronounced in speech.

It is also said: it was omitted because of frequent use, for lightness; and because it was used frequently they found it easy to omit it, unlike His saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ and its like, since there the usage was not frequent.

Then they differed about the derivation of the word ism (name). Al-Mubarrad and a group of the Basrans said: ism is derived from sumuww, which means height and manifestation, so it is as if it manifests its meaning and rises above it, and its meaning becomes beneath it.

Tha'lab, from the Kufans, said: it is derived from wasm and simah (mark), so it is as if it is a sign for its meaning. The first is more preferable, because the diminutive of ism is formed on the named (suwayy'); and if it were derived from sa'ah (breadth), its diminutive would be formed on wusayy, as it is said of wasl: wusayl, and of wa'd: wu'ayd.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah﴾, the Exalted, the scholars have differed about it. Al-Khalil and Ibn Kaysan said it is a proper name specific to Allah the Exalted, with no derivation, and it is like the proper names of people, such as Zayd, 'Amr, and the like. This is the choice of al-Qaffal al-Shashi and a group of scholars.

The rest said it is a derived name, and concerning the point of derivation there are two opinions. The first: that it is derived from their saying: alaha ilahatan, meaning he worshipped with worship. Ibn 'Abbas recited: "wa-yadharaka wa-ilahatak", meaning your worship.

The devout worshipper is called mata'alih, and from this is the saying of the poet:

(Glory be to them, and they returned from one who worships)

meaning: one who worships. So its meaning is that He is the One deserving worship, to Him all acts of worship are directed, and He is the One worshipped, so none other is to be worshipped.

It is also said: al-Ilah is the one who is the Creator of creation, the Provider for them, the Manager of their affairs, the One Empowered over them.

The second: that "Allah" originally is ilah, and the origin of ilah is wilah, except that the waw was replaced by a hamza, like their saying: washah and ishah.

Its derivation is from the wilah (bewilderment), as if the servants are bewildered toward Allah, turning to Him, humbling themselves, and seeking refuge in Him in hardships.

As for His saying: ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: they are two tender names, one of them more tender than the other.

It is also related from him that he said: "al-Rahman" is the Gentle toward the servants, and "al-Rahim" is the Compassionate toward them. Then they differed about it. Some said: "al-Rahman" is other than "al-Rahim," and each of them has a meaning different from the other's. Others said: they are one.

As for the one who said "al-Rahman" is other than "al-Rahim," he said: al-Rahman has the meaning of generality, and al-Rahim has the meaning of specificity. On this basis, "al-Rahman" means the Provider in this world, and provision is general, for the disbeliever and the believer; and "al-Rahim" means the Pardoner in the Hereafter, and pardon in the Hereafter is specific to the believers without the disbelievers. For this reason it is said in supplication: "O Rahman of this world and Rahim of the next." So "al-Rahman" is one whose mercy reaches creation generally, and "al-Rahim" is one whose mercy reaches creation specifically; for this reason one may call other than Allah "rahim" but not "rahman," because Allah the Exalted is the One whose mercy reaches creation, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾. As for other than Allah, He may single out something for mercy, and thereby be merciful.

As for the one who said their meaning is one: Qutrub said: they are two names, one of them mentioned, ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾, as an emphasis for the other, like: lahfan and lahif, nadman and nadim.

Al-Mubarrad said: "this is completion after completion, and favour after favour, and an enticement for the hearts of those who desire, and a promise that does not disappoint its hope." Its meaning is: the One possessing mercy, and mercy is bounty and favour.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 1, verse 2:

His words: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾. Know that al-hamd (praise) may mean gratitude for a favour, and it may mean commendation and extolling of praiseworthy attributes. It is said: "I praised so-and-so for what he bestowed upon me of favour." And it is said: "I praised so-and-so for his bravery and his knowledge." As for shukr (thanks), it is only for a favour; so hamd has a general meaning and shukr has a specific meaning. Every one who praises is thankful, but not every one who is thankful praises.

It is said: "I praised so-and-so for his bravery." But it is not said: "I thanked so-and-so for his bravery."

Then know that Allah, exalted is He, praising Himself is good, unlike the praise of created beings for themselves; because the praise of created beings is never free from deficiency, so their self-praise is never free from falsehood, and so it is ugly for them to praise themselves. As for Allah, majestic is His majesty, He is free from deficiency and defect, so His praising Himself is good.

His words: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ here may bear two meanings: informing, and teaching. As for informing, it is as if He informs that the one deserving of praise is Allah, and that all praiseworthy qualities belong to Allah, exalted is He.

As for teaching, it is as if He praises Himself and teaches His servants His praise, and its implied meaning is: "Say: All praise is due to Allah."

His words: ﴿to Allah﴾: the lam (preposition "to/for") may indicate idafa (possession/attribution), and it may indicate istihqaq (entitlement). It is said: "food for the animal" and "the house is for Zayd." So the lam here carries the meaning of entitlement, as if He says: the one entitled to praise is Allah, exalted is He. We have already finished explaining His words: ﴿to Allah﴾.

﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. As for rabb (lord), it may mean nurturing and reforming, and it may mean owner. It is said: "rabb al-day'a yurabbīhā," meaning he completed it and set it right. And it is said: "rabb al-dar" meaning the owner of the house. So rabb here bears both meanings, because Allah is the nurturer of the worlds and the owner of the worlds.

As for ﴿the worlds﴾ (al-'alamin): Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the jinn and mankind. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Abu 'Ubayda said: they are all created beings. It is said: the first is more apt, because the address is with those who are responsible (mukallafun), who are the intended recipients of the caliphate, and they are the jinn and humankind. It is also said: mankind is one world, and the jinn is one world. And Allah, exalted is He, has beyond them four corners, in each corner one thousand five hundred worlds.
We have already finished explaining ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. He mentioned it a second time for the purpose of emphasis.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 1, verse 4:

His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ is recited in two readings: "Māliki" and "Maliki" (mālik and malik). Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī said: "Mālik" with the alif is preferable, because it is broader and more comprehensive. It is said: mālik al-dār (owner of the house), mālik al-ṭayr (owner of the birds), mālik al-ʿabd (owner of the slave), and the noun "malik" (king) is not derived from it.

Abū ʿUbayd and al-Mubarrad said: "Malik" (king) is preferable, because it is more complete, for "al-malik" (the king) comprises the meaning of "al-mālik" (the owner), whereas "al-mālik" does not comprise the meaning of "al-malik", for every king is an owner, but not every owner is a king. Also, it is more in harmony with the wording of the Qur'an, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King﴾, and His saying: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾, and similar verses. So "mālik" is derived from "al-mulk" and "al-mulkah" (dominion and sovereignty), and "malik" is derived from "al-mulk" and "al-mulkah". Allah, may He be exalted, is both Mālik and Malik.

As for ﴿the Day﴾, it is the name of a known time. What is meant by "Yawm al-Dīn" is the Day of Resurrection, and its meaning is the Day of Reckoning and the Day of Recompense. The word "dīn" may also mean obedience and [the sense of] ... [text here is corrupt in the source], but here it bears one of the two meanings. If someone asks: why was the Day of Judgment singled out for mention, when Allah, may He be exalted, is the Owner of all days? It is said: He singled it out because the command on the Resurrection Day belongs wholly to Him, as He said: ﴿And the command on that Day belongs to Allah﴾. As for in this world, there is a command for kings, a command for Muslims, and a command for prophets.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 1, verse 5:

His saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.﴾ His saying: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ means: We worship You. Ibadah ('ibadah, worship) is obedience combined with humility and submission. It is said: "a paved road" (tariq mu'abbad), meaning one that has been made smooth (mudhallal). Its meaning is: We worship You in submission.

﴿And You alone we ask for help﴾ means: we seek assistance from You. If it is asked: Why is the mention of worship placed before seeking help? Should not seeking help come before worship? And why is "You alone" (iyyaka) mentioned twice, when it would have sufficed to say: "You alone we worship and seek help from"? For that is more concise and more succinct. It is answered: As for the first, it applies only to one who holds that the capacity (istita'ah) precedes the act. But we, by the praise of God, hold that seeking help and divine success (tawfiq) accompany the act, whether it is coupled with it or placed after it, and both are permissible.

Or it is said: Because seeking help is a kind of worship, so he mentioned the whole of worship and then mentioned what is among its details.

As for His saying: ﴿And You alone we ask for help﴾, He repeated it because if He had restricted Himself to saying "You alone we worship and seek help," it would have been known that He is the one worshipped and the one sought for help. Also, the Arabs do speak in this manner: a statement may be made with emphasis (tajrid) or for magnification and exaltation (tafkhim wa ta'zim), and this is not considered a defect. As the Arabs say: "This is the owner, between Zayd and 'Amr," although the statement "The wealth is between Zayd and 'Amr" conveys the same meaning as the first. This is not considered a defect in speech; rather, it is counted as magnification and grandeur in speech.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 1, verse 6:

His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ means: direct us and make us firm.

Guidance (al-hidayah) in the Qur'an has several meanings. Guidance may mean inspiration (al-ilham), it may mean direction (al-irshad), it may mean clarification (al-bayan), and it may mean invitation (al-du'a').

As for inspiration, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation and then guided it﴾, meaning: inspired it.

As for direction, His saying the Exalted: ﴿And guide us to the even path﴾.

As for clarification, His saying: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾, meaning: We made clear to them.

As for invitation, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾, meaning: a caller. So here it carries the sense of seeking guidance (al-istirshad).

If someone says: what is the meaning of seeking guidance, when every believer is already guided? So what is the meaning of His saying ﴿guide us﴾? We say: this question comes from one who holds that the divine favours (al-alutaf) of Allah the Exalted are finite. The school of the People of the Sunnah holds that the favours and guidances from Allah the Exalted are not finite. Thus it means seeking an increase in guidance, and it also means a request for firmness: "guide us" means "make us firm," just as one says to someone standing: "Stand until I return to you," meaning: remain standing.

As for ﴿the straight path﴾, 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud said: it is Islam. Jabir said: it is the Qur'an. Its original meaning in the language is: the clear road, and Islam is a clear road, and the Qur'an is a clear road.

And the poet said:

(The Commander of the Faithful is upon a path... when the watering-places are crooked, it is straight)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 1, verse 7:

His saying ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who have gone astray﴾. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "The path of those whom You have favoured, not of those who have incurred anger, and not of those who have gone astray." However, this is among the shadhdh (irregular, non-canonical readings), and the well-known recitation is the familiar one.

It has been said: "Those upon whom You have bestowed favour" are the prophets. It has also been said: they are everyone whom Allah has made firm upon faith among the prophets and believers, all of them.

Abu al-'Aliya al-Riyahi said: they are the Messenger, Abu Bakr, and Umar.

As for His saying ﴿not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who have gone astray﴾, then "amin". The ones who have incurred anger are the Jews, and the ones who have gone astray are the Christians.

It is related from 'Adi ibn Hatim that he came to the Prophet to embrace Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are those who have incurred anger?" He said: "The Jews." He said: "And who are those who have gone astray?" He said: "The Christians." 'Adi said: "I bear witness that I am a true believer, a Muslim." 'Adi said: "I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah brighten and smile, joyful at my Islam."

As for "amin", it is not part of the Qur'an. The Sunnah for the reciter is to pause briefly and then say: "Amin."

It has two forms: "Amin" with a long vowel (amin, with madd), and "Amin" with a short vowel (amin, qasr). Its meaning is: "O Allah, answer." It has also been said that it is the seal of supplication.
